first.rationale: The two live symptoms are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing it plausibly recovers both; memory_86 and memory_31 both point at shortening/simplifying the self-serve path as a durable lift. I am spending verification on memory_86 (the load-bearing evidence for my chosen action) and memory_91 (the strongest alternative, activation messaging), because those are the two pulls that could actually flip the decision. I deliberately decline promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing being the loudest signal this week: memory_73 records that it bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and explicitly warns against generalizing it, which is disqualifying against a sustainable long-term qualified-revenue objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but target established customers and do nothing for the two declining metrics. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is orthogonal to a self-serve activation problem. Downstream risks I am flagging rather than assuming away: (a) stripping signup fields can degrade lead qualification and routing, which would quietly damage pipeline quality even as activation numbers improve, and memory_44 implies enterprise prospects should stay on the sales-assisted path, so the simplification must be scoped to self-serve/SMB and not cannibalize the demo-request flow; (b) 'completion' and 'activation' can be inflated by making the funnel easier without improving real time-to-value, so I want retention and qualified-pipeline guardrails, not just completion rate. Uncertainty I am not collapsing: these memories are compressed summaries carrying no effect sizes, no baselines, and no confidence intervals, and they are 15-45 days old; nothing in the record establishes that the same mechanism explains the current QoQ declines, which could instead stem from traffic-mix shift caused by the competitor pulling price-sensitive accounts. Verification of memory_86 is meant to test exactly that. If the archived record shows the original onboarding win was small, short-lived, or confounded, I would switch to activation_messaging (memory_91) as the cheaper, more reversible intervention.

final.rationale: Both pulls came back confirmed, so neither flipped the decision, and the tiebreak now rests on effect size plus position in the funnel. exp_86 shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%; exp_91 shows activation +6% with retention +1%. Onboarding is the larger effect, carries the better retention signal, and sits upstream of activation, so recovering it plausibly addresses both the -4% completion and a meaningful share of the -6% activation decline. Activation messaging remains the strong runner-up and the natural next slot. One thing the archive clarified and I am updating on: exp_86 was a shortened onboarding flow, not the signup-field reduction described in memory_31. Those are adjacent but distinct interventions, and only the former is verified. I am therefore scoping this experiment to shortening the onboarding flow itself and explicitly NOT stripping signup fields, since the lead-qualification and routing risk I flagged earlier attaches to the unverified memory_31 variant, not to the verified one. I continue to decline promotional_pricing even though the competitor's entry pricing is the most urgent-feeling pressure: memory_73 records real acquisition and revenue lift bought at the cost of 30-day retention, with an explicit instruction not to generalize it, and the objective here is sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Matching a competitor on price would trade the exact metric the verified onboarding work protects. referral_incentive (memory_57) is clean but aimed at established customers and does not touch either declining metric; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is orthogonal to a self-serve funnel problem. Residual risks I am carrying rather than dismissing: the shortened flow must not divert enterprise prospects off the sales-assisted demo path that memory_44 says converts better, so I will segment self-serve/SMB and leave the demo-request route untouched; and completion rate is gameable by simply removing friction without delivering value, so I will hold 30-day retention, time-to-value, and qualified pipeline as guardrails rather than reading completion alone. Uncertainty I am not collapsing: exp_86 confirms the intervention worked on day 52's population, but nothing in the archive establishes that the same mechanism explains the current quarter's declines. The competitor pulling price-sensitive accounts may have shifted traffic mix, in which case the historical lift will not fully replicate. I expect a partial, not full, recovery and will treat a null result as evidence for the mix-shift hypothesis rather than as a failure of the onboarding change.
